guide.summary: Slack uses a standard v2 OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow. Creating an app and getting a token is quick. Distributing it commercially is the hard part. Slack's API Terms say the Marketplace is the only appropriate channel for commercial distribution. Apps outside the Marketplace are throttled hard on conversations.history and conversations.replies. Marketplace review requires 10 or more active workspaces before you can submit, and functional review can take up to 10 weeks with no expediting.
auth_alternatives: oauth.v2.user.access (user-centric endpoint): Slack intends this for MCP flows. Choose it when your agent only needs user tokens, not a bot token. The trade-off is that you get no bot identity.

Internal customer-built app: choose this when a customer builds the app for their own workspace. It keeps higher conversations.history/replies limits (1,000 objects per request, 50+ requests per minute). The trade-off is that it cannot be distributed commercially.
Sign in with Slack (OpenID Connect): choose this for identity or login only. The discovery document advertises a separate authorize endpoint. It is not a substitute for API access tokens.

reasons_to_bring_own: Commercial distribution under your own app name: Slack's API Terms say the Marketplace is the only appropriate channel for commercially distributed apps, including unlisted apps. Owning that path means your own app and review.
You need scopes that a managed app has not had approved. Published apps fail with unapproved_scope for scopes that have not passed review.
GovSlack customers: GovSlack apps use the slack-gov.com host instead of slack.com.
A customer wants the higher rate limits that internal customer-built apps keep. That requires an app built in their own workspace.
build_or_borrow.verdict: Use Composio managed auth to start, because your own app would face the 10-active-workspace Marketplace prerequisite, a review of up to 10 weeks, and severe rate limits on message history if it is distributed outside the Marketplace.

For Marketplace review: a short demo video, required for new submissions and for updates that add functionality or scopes.

oauth.token_lifetime: Tokens do not expire by default. Optional token rotation issues an expiring access token plus a refresh token. The authorization code expires after ten minutes.

Configured under OAuth & Permissions on the App Management page.

blockers.text: Marketplace submission is blocked until the app is installed on 10 or more workspaces active in the past 28 days.
blockers.workaround: Activate public distribution and get design partners to install the app first. Alternatively, start with Composio managed auth.

blockers.text: Non-Marketplace commercially distributed apps are limited to 1 request per minute and 15 objects per request on conversations.history and conversations.replies. This applies to new apps and installs after May 29, 2025.
blockers.workaround: Plan for Marketplace listing if your agent reads message history. Otherwise design around the throttle.

blockers.text: Functional review takes up to 10 weeks for new submissions, and Slack will not expedite it for a launch.
blockers.workaround: Submit well before any launch date and keep the requested scopes minimal.

blockers.text: Marketplace apps may not request broad or restricted scopes such as search:read and admin.*.
blockers.workaround: Design features around narrower scopes before you submit.

blockers.text: Workspace admins can restrict installs to admins only or to Marketplace apps, or can require approval of install requests.
blockers.workaround: Tell users their admin may need to approve the install. A Marketplace listing helps where installs are limited to Marketplace apps.

steps.title: Create the Slack app
steps.detail_md:
Sign in and create the app on the App Management page (https://api.slack.com/apps). Copy the client ID from that page; you will also need the client secret for the token exchange.

A new app can only be installed in the workspace it was created in. Other workspaces need the OAuth flow, which later steps cover.

steps.title: Draft the scope list (bot vs user)
steps.detail_md:
The agent drafts the smallest scope set the integration needs, split into bot scopes (`scope` parameter) and user scopes (`user_scope` parameter).

Keep it tight from day one:
- Scopes are additive across installs. You cannot shrink a token's scopes without revoking it.
- Changing scopes later forces every workspace to reinstall.
- If you plan to list on the Marketplace, do not request legacy, restricted or broad-access scopes such as `search:read` or `admin.*`.

The developer signs off on the final list.

steps.title: Decide on token rotation and PKCE (irreversible)
steps.detail_md:
Once enabled, token rotation and PKCE cannot be turned off, so the developer makes this call. The agent can only lay out the options.

- **Default:** tokens do not expire. This is simpler to run, but a leaked token stays valid.
- **Rotation on:** you get a refresh token and an expiring access token. You must build and run refresh logic, permanently.

The OpenID discovery probe did not advertise PKCE methods, so test PKCE before you rely on it.

steps.title: Prepare redirect URLs
steps.detail_md:
The agent lists the redirect URLs for each environment. Rules:
- HTTPS only.
- No `#` anchor.
- Matching is by prefix: a `redirect_uri` can be the configured URL or a subdirectory of it. Register narrow paths so you do not over-allow.

Once the app is distributed, its interactivity, options load and Events API URLs also need SSL.

steps.title: Enter redirect URLs in the dashboard
steps.detail_md: Add the redirect URLs under **OAuth & Permissions** on the App Management page.

steps.title: Write the OAuth integration code
steps.detail_md:
The agent writes the integration code.

**Authorize**
- Send users to `https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize` with `scope` and/or `user_scope`.
- GovSlack apps use slack-gov.com instead.

**Token exchange**
- Exchange the code at `https://slack.com/api/oauth.v2.access` using the client secret.
- Do it promptly: the code expires after ten minutes.
- If you only need user tokens (for example an MCP-style flow), Slack offers `oauth.v2.user.access`.

**Rate limits**
- Handle HTTP 429 by honoring the `Retry-After` header.

The authorize endpoint was probed and responded with HTTP 200.

Composio offers managed auth for Slack if you would rather not run this flow yourself.

steps.title: Test install in your own workspace
steps.detail_md: Run the full flow in the app's own workspace and confirm both bot and user tokens work.

steps.title: Decide your distribution path
steps.detail_md:
This is the key decision for an AI agent. The developer makes it.

**What the terms say**
- Slack's API Terms say the Marketplace is the only appropriate channel for commercially distributing apps, including unlisted ones.
- Unlisted apps are for development and testing.

**What it means for rate limits**
- Commercially distributed apps outside the Marketplace get `conversations.history` and `conversations.replies` capped at 1 request per minute and 15 objects per request. This applies to new apps and new installs after May 29, 2025.
- Internal customer-built apps keep higher limits (1,000 objects per request, 50+ requests per minute).
- Slack says the change targets unsanctioned data scraping, including by AI systems.

**Bottom line:** a commercial agent that reads message history should plan for the Marketplace.

steps.title: Activate public distribution
steps.detail_md:
In the app dashboard, open **Manage Distribution**, complete the checklist, and click **Activate Public Distribution**. This is what lets other workspaces install the app.

Be aware before you do it:
- Deactivating later removes the app from every workspace except the original one.
- Once the app is published on the Marketplace, you cannot deactivate at all.

steps.title: Get to 10 active workspaces
steps.detail_md:
Marketplace review is blocked until the app is installed on 10 or more active workspaces. Active means used within the past 28 days.

Plan for workspace admin rules:
- Admins may limit installs to admins only, or to Marketplace-listed apps.
- Admins may require approval, in which case users submit install requests for review.

The agent can draft install instructions that cover these cases.

How long this takes depends entirely on your users and is not documented. The estimate below covers only your outreach effort.

steps.title: Prepare submission materials
steps.detail_md:
The agent drafts the listing copy, a justification for each scope, and a script for the short demo video that new submissions require.

Slack charges nothing for Marketplace inclusion, but it runs a security review and analyzes every requested scope.

steps.title: Record the demo video and submit for review
steps.detail_md: Record the demo video and submit the app for Marketplace review.

steps.title: Preliminary review
steps.detail_md: Slack gives preliminary feedback within up to 10 business days (roughly two calendar weeks). Slack will not expedite review to match a launch date.

steps.title: Functional review
steps.detail_md:
Functional review takes up to 10 weeks for a new submission. Resubmissions of published apps take up to 6 weeks. Do not schedule a launch inside this window.

Until scopes are approved, installing the published app fails with `unapproved_scope`.

steps.title: Operate after publication
steps.detail_md:
After publication the live app is locked. Rules for the integration code:
- Never add unreviewed scopes to the install link. Doing so causes install errors (`unapproved_scope`).
- New scopes or functionality need another review with a demo video. Resubmissions take up to 6 weeks.
- Changing scopes means workspaces must reinstall.

drivers: up to 10 week functional review, no expediting

belief_diff.topic: Does letting arbitrary users connect require provider review or verification?
belief_diff.prior_belief: Yes, Slack requires app directory submission and review before any workspace outside the developer's own can install a distributed app publicly.
belief_diff.finding: Claims say a newly created app installs only in its home workspace and other installs need OAuth, and that Marketplace publication involves security review, but they do not state that review is required before any outside workspace can install; unlisted apps are described as intended for development and testing, which partly aligns but does not confirm the gating rule.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Slack's directory review typically takes about 2 to 4 weeks from submission to approval.
belief_diff.finding: Claims give preliminary feedback up to 10 business days and functional review up to 10 weeks for new submissions (6 weeks for resubmissions), which contradicts the 2 to 4 week estimate as a typical range.

belief_diff.topic: Limits while the app is unapproved
belief_diff.prior_belief: An unlisted distributed app can still be installed by any workspace via its install link, but it is capped at 25 workspace installations before directory listing is required.
belief_diff.finding: Claims contain no 25-installation cap; they state unlisted apps are for development and testing, commercial distribution must go through the Marketplace, and non-Marketplace commercial apps face reduced conversations.history limits.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Creating and distributing a Slack app is free, with no fee, though paid Marketplace listings are not supported and apps cannot charge through Slack.
belief_diff.finding: Claims state Slack does not charge for Marketplace inclusion, but say nothing about paid listings or in-app charging.

belief_diff.topic: Key prerequisites (domain, privacy policy, video, business verification)
belief_diff.prior_belief: Submission requires a verified company domain, a public privacy policy URL, a support contact, and a demo video, but no separate business verification process.
belief_diff.finding: Claims confirm a short demo video is required for new submissions and that SSL is required for distributed app URLs, plus a 10-workspace, 28-day-active install threshold; they do not mention a verified domain, privacy policy, support contact, or business verification.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Redirect URIs must use HTTPS, except localhost for development, and must exactly match one of the URLs registered in the app's OAuth settings.
belief_diff.finding: Claims say redirect URIs must use HTTPS and match a configured URL or a subdirectory of it as a prefix match, not an exact match; no localhost exception is mentioned, and anchors are disallowed.
